panels.title: Big questions
points: How can I tell what a writer from 1860 really thinks?

panels.title: Islamic foundation
panels.text: Islam teaches that patience (sabr, صَبْر) is a strength, not a weakness: 'O you who have believed, seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, Allah is with the patient' (al-Baqarah 2:153). Both of today's texts are about waiting, discomfort and keeping steady on a hard journey, so pupils can test the writers' views against this teaching.

panels.title: Text Two: reading a nineteenth-century writer's perspective
points: translate difficult phrases into modern English
state the writer's perspective with evidence
explain how tone and sentence forms convey that perspective

panels.title: How does the writer present his advice to travellers? (10 marks)
points: Perspective: travellers must accept the sea's power with patience
Evidence: 'the sea will consult his convenience' (negated by 'Let no traveller suppose')
Method: the formal imperative gives the voice of experienced authority
Effect: the reader is warned, but gently mocked for expecting comfort
Answer: The writer presents his advice with the confident authority of experience, using formal imperatives and the metaphor of a 'stern schoolmaster' to show that hardship teaches.
